title: Pairing flow: node-side implementation
description:
Implement full server-side pairing flow per spec §1.5.

Flow:
1. Receive pair_client_hello → validate version, suite selection
2. Send pair_server_hello with selected suite + enroll_id
3. Compute pair_context, pair_aad
4. Receive pair_init (pA) → compute SPAKE2 server side (pB)
5. Send pair_resp (pB)
6. Derive Ke, Ka, KcA, KcB per RFC 9382
7. Receive pair_confirm1 → verify client MAC. On failure: decrement attempts, send pair_error
8. Send pair_confirm2 with server MAC
9. Derive boot_c2s, boot_s2c, boot_export via HKDF from Ke
10. Encrypt bootstrap payload (node_id, noise_static_pubkey, etc.) with ChaCha20-Poly1305 under boot_s2c
11. Send pair_bootstrap
12. Receive pair_done → mark enrollment used, destroy

Error handling: wrong MAC → decrement attempts_left, attempts_exhausted → destroy enrollment.

title: Event-sourced session state projection for idle detection
description:
Currently consumeCodexOutput makes side-effect decisions (thread/unsubscribe) inside an imperative loop by checking meta fields. This is fragile — event ordering from Codex is not guaranteed (e.g. session.state.changed(ready) can arrive before or after turn.completed), causing sessions to hang as 'running' forever.

Replace with proper event-sourced projection:
1. Define SessionProjectionState derived from persisted orchestration events (has turn completed? is session ready? is there an active turn?)
2. After each event is persisted, recompute projection
3. Side-effect manager checks projection and triggers actions (unsubscribe, cleanup, notify) idempotently
4. Remove event-specific conditionals from consumeCodexOutput — it should only parse and persist, not decide
5. Works correctly regardless of event ordering, multi-node, or daemon restart (projection rebuilt from persisted events)

This fixes the current bug where Codex sessions hang as 'running' after completion because turn.completed arrives after session.state.changed(ready).

title: Transport: hello negotiation + prologue binding
description:

Messages:
- client_hello: { t, v, noise_suites[], node_id, expected_key_id, app_protocols[], features[] }
- server_hello: { t, v, noise_suite, node_id, key_id, app_protocol, features[], max_frame }
- transport_error: { t, code: unsupported_version|unsupported_suite|no_such_node|key_id_mismatch|protocol_error }

Prologue computation:
  transcript = CanonicalJSON(client_hello) || CanonicalJSON(server_hello)
  prologue = 'orka-transport/v1' || relay_origin || transcript

Key ID validation: if expected_key_id \!= actual key_id, server responds with key_id_mismatch error.

Zod schemas for all messages + prologue computation function.

title: [epic] Smart transport: relay hardening, LAN discovery, optimal routing
description:
Make orka transport layer smart about network topology. Three pillars:

1. **Relay hardening** — improve existing relay for production use: reconnect resilience, auth improvements, connection draining, health monitoring.

2. **LAN/Tailscale discovery** — daemon nodes advertise themselves on the local network (mDNS/DNS-SD or custom UDP broadcast). Clients discover nearby daemons without manual --remote configuration. Works across physical LAN and Tailscale/WireGuard mesh networks.

3. **Optimal path selection** — when multiple paths exist to the same daemon (direct LAN, Tailscale, relay), the client should measure RTT and prefer the fastest route. Fallback chain: direct > Tailscale > relay.

Security requirements:
- All paths must be encrypted (E2E encryption already exists for relay; direct connections need mutual TLS or equivalent)
- Discovery must not leak session content — only advertise node ID and public key
- Nodes must authenticate to each other before exchanging data
- Phone/mobile clients connecting via Tailscale should work seamlessly

Use case: user on phone discovers their home workstation daemon via Tailscale, connects directly with sub-ms RTT instead of routing through a cloud relay.

title: SaaS: CI/CD integration (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI)
description:
First-class integration with CI/CD pipelines so teams can spawn agent sessions from their existing workflows.

## What it is
A GitHub Action (and GitLab CI template) that spawns an Orka agent session as part of a CI pipeline. Use cases: automated code review, test generation, bug fix attempts, documentation generation, migration scripts.

## Architecture changes needed
1. **GitHub Action**: A reusable action that installs Orka CLI, connects to user's relay, spawns a session, waits for completion, and reports results as PR comment or check annotation.
2. **Stateless spawn**: CI environments are ephemeral. The action uses --remote to connect to the user's relay and spawn on a managed node. No local tmux needed.
3. **Result extraction**: After session completes, extract result via `orka result --json`, post as PR comment, create a branch with changes, or fail the CI check.
4. **Webhook triggers**: Optionally, relay can call a webhook when session completes (for async CI workflows).
5. **GitHub App**: For tighter integration — auto-spawn agent on PR creation, comment with results, push fix branches.

## Revenue model
- Free for open source (spawn on own nodes)
- Pro/Team includes CI credits (100 CI sessions/month)
- Enterprise: unlimited CI sessions, GitHub Enterprise Server support
- This drives adoption of managed compute (CI needs ephemeral nodes)

## Privacy implications
- CI secrets (API keys) need secure injection — use GitHub Actions secrets → Orka encrypted config
- E2E encryption works: CI runner encrypts, managed node decrypts
- Code is already on GitHub, so the privacy bar is lower for CI use case

## Implementation complexity
- Medium. The core is just a shell script wrapping `orka spawn --remote`. The GitHub App is more work.
- High value for adoption — makes Orka useful even for teams that don't use it day-to-day.

title: Research sandbox/isolation for agent sessions (like t3 code)
description:
Research and implement sandboxing/isolation for agent sessions. Currently agents run with full filesystem/network access.

## Isolation approaches to research

### Docker containers
- Per-session Docker container with mounted worktree
- Pre-built image with all tools (git, bun, node, claude, codex)
- Network isolation (no access to host network unless allowed)
- Resource limits (CPU, memory, disk)

### Devcontainers
- Use devcontainer.json from the project repo
- Leverage existing devcontainer ecosystem
- Agent runs inside the dev environment the project already defines
- Works with VS Code Remote Containers, GitHub Codespaces

### Container runtimes per platform
- **Linux**: Docker (native), Podman (rootless alternative)
- **macOS**: Colima (lightweight, recommended), OrbStack (commercial alternative), Docker Desktop (heavy)
- **Windows**: Docker Desktop, WSL2 + Docker, Podman
- Must abstract runtime — orka shouldn't care if it's docker/colima/podman underneath
- Discovery via orka-3wwx (node capability detection) determines what's available
- Setup wizard: suggest and help install appropriate runtime per OS

### Other system tools
- Bubblewrap (bwrap) — lightweight namespace-based sandboxing
- Firejail — easy sandboxing for CLI apps
- seccomp/landlock — kernel-level syscall filtering
- Filesystem overlays (overlayfs) — copy-on-write for worktree

### Backend-native sandbox

- Delegating to the backend vs wrapping at orka level

1. **Untrusted prompts** — run agent tasks from external sources safely
2. **Supervisor sessions** — supervisor spawns workers in sandboxes
3. **Non-worktree sessions** — supervisor itself runs without worktree, directly in project dir
4. **Fleet security** — ensure remote nodes can't escape their sandbox
5. **Reproducibility** — consistent environment across nodes

Design doc with:
- Comparison of approaches (security, performance, DX, portability)
- Recommended approach (probably Docker + devcontainer support)
- How it integrates with orka spawn (--sandbox, --container, --devcontainer flags)
- How it interacts with worktrees (mount worktree into container?)
- Session types: worktree (current), in-place (no worktree), containerized
- Container runtime abstraction (docker/colima/podman — unified interface)
- Per-platform runtime recommendations and setup flow
- Performance impact analysis

title: Share sessions via temporary access link (read-only and read-write)
description:
Allow sharing a session with someone via a temporary link/token. Two modes:
1. Read-only: viewer sees live session output, timeline, diff — but can't send input or stop
2. Read-write: full access to send follow-ups, stop, etc.

Link format: https://orka.example.com/shared/<token>
Token: short-lived (configurable TTL, default 24h), revocable, scoped to one session.

Use cases: show a colleague what an agent is doing, pair on debugging, let a reviewer see the diff.

## Authentication & Authorization
- Share tokens ARE the auth mechanism for shared access (bearer token)
- Token validation on EVERY RPC call, not just connection
- RW token holders can only: sendTurn, stop — NOT delete, merge, archive, change settings
- RO token holders can only: read timeline, read diff, read status
- Token scoped to single session — no access to other sessions or workspace
- Token revocation takes effect immediately (check on every request, not just connect)
- Rate limiting per token to prevent abuse
- Audit log: who accessed, when, what actions

## Event attribution (user-initiated events only)
For read-write sharing, user-initiated events need actor attribution:
- user.input: `actor: { id: string; name?: string; type: 'owner' | 'shared' }`
- session.stopped / session.cancelled: same actor field
- NOT on system/agent events — those have no human actor
- Dashboard shows who sent each message (like a shared chat)

## Implementation
- Token DB: session_share_tokens (token, session_id, mode, actor_name, created_by, expires_at, revoked_at)
- RPC: createShareToken, revokeShareToken, listShareTokens
- Auth middleware: validate token per-request, inject actor context
- sendTurn RPC: accepts optional actor, propagated to user.input event
- Dashboard: shared view (minimal UI, no sidebar, session-focused)
- Relay: share tokens work through relay for remote sessions

title: Node capability discovery — detect installed tools, agents, and runtimes
description:
When a node connects to the fleet, we need to know what's available on it. Currently we blindly try to spawn agents and fail if the backend isn't installed.

## What to discover

### Agent backends
- Claude Code (claude CLI) — version, config location, login status
- Codex (codex CLI) — version, available models
- Future backends

### Container runtimes
- Docker (docker / docker-compose) — version, running?
- Colima (macOS) — running? docker context set up?
- Podman — version
- OrbStack (macOS alternative)
- Devcontainer CLI (@devcontainers/cli)
- Windows: WSL2, Docker Desktop

### System tools
- Git — version, config
- Bun / Node.js — version
- Python — version (for some tools)
- SSH — for remote operations

### Platform info
- OS (Linux/macOS/Windows), arch (x64/arm64)
- Available RAM, CPU cores, disk space
- Network: can reach relay? can reach API endpoints?

## Discovery modes

### 1. On connect (initial)
- Full scan when node first connects to relay
- Report all capabilities

### 2. Continuous / periodic
- Re-scan on a configurable interval (e.g. every 5 minutes)
- Detect newly installed or removed tools without daemon restart
- Watch for container runtime start/stop (Colima started, Docker stopped, etc.)

### 3. On demand
- CLI: `orka discover` triggers immediate re-scan
- Dashboard: refresh button on fleet inventory page
- Before spawn: quick check if required backend is still available

### 4. Event-driven
- Detect tool install/uninstall via filesystem watchers (PATH changes)
- Container runtime status changes
- OS-level package manager hooks (optional, advanced)

## Features
1. **Auto-discovery on daemon start** — scan for installed tools, cache result
2. **Continuous monitoring** — periodic re-scan, push updates to relay
3. **Report to relay** — nodes advertise capabilities, relay shows fleet inventory
4. **Smart routing** — supervisor/spawn can target nodes by capability (e.g. 'needs docker')
5. **Missing tool suggestions** — if user tries to spawn codex on a node without it: 'Codex not found. Install with: npm i -g @openai/codex'
6. **Container runtime setup wizard** — detect OS, suggest appropriate runtime (Docker on Linux, Colima on macOS, Docker Desktop on Windows)
7. **Dashboard view** — fleet inventory page showing per-node capabilities, live status
8. **Capability diff notifications** — alert when a node loses or gains a capability

## API
- Node reports capabilities on connect and periodically: `{ backends: ['claude-code'], containers: ['docker'], os: 'linux', arch: 'x64', ... }`
- RPC: `getNodeCapabilities(nodeId)` — returns full capability report
- RPC: `discoverCapabilities()` — triggers re-scan on a node
- Relay aggregates: `getFleetCapabilities()` — all nodes with live status
- Push: `capabilities.updated` — broadcast when node capabilities change

## Integration
- `orka spawn --backend codex` checks if target node has codex before dispatching
- Supervisor agent uses capabilities to route tasks to appropriate nodes
- Dashboard shows warning icons for nodes missing expected tools
- Sandbox task (orka-3lk) uses discovery to know which container runtime is available

title: Type-safe RPC client — derive method names from OrkaService interface
description:

2. Add a type helper: `function rpc<M extends keyof OrkaService>(method: M, params: Parameters<OrkaService[M]>[0]): Promise<ReturnType<OrkaService[M]>>`
3. Reuse OrkaClient from @orka/client directly in dashboard (it already has typed methods)

title: Derive chat input state from orchestration events
description:

**File: packages/dashboard/src/components/ChatView.tsx** (or extract to a hook)

Create a function/hook: useInputState(events, sessionStatus, backend)

Logic:
```
if session is in terminal state (completed/failed/cancelled):
  return 'disabled'
if no events yet and session is queued/preparing:
  return 'not_started'
if last turn event is turn.started (no matching turn.completed):
  return 'busy'
if last turn event is turn.completed and session is still running:
  return 'waiting'
default:
  return 'disabled'
```

Edge cases:
- Session just created, first turn hasn't started -> 'not_started' until first turn starts, then 'busy'
- Multiple rapid turns (agent auto-continues) -> 'busy' until the last turn completes
- item.started without turn context -> still 'busy' (tool execution in progress)

title: SaaS: Team collaboration (RBAC, shared relay, audit)
description:
Multi-user team features: shared relay namespace, role-based access control, audit logging.

## What it is
Teams share a relay namespace where multiple users can see each other's sessions, share nodes, and manage permissions. An admin can control who can spawn sessions, which nodes they can use, and review an audit trail.

## Architecture changes needed
1. **Team/org model**: Account hierarchy: Org → Teams → Users. Stored in relay's Postgres.
2. **RBAC**: Roles: owner, admin, member, viewer. Permissions: spawn sessions, view all sessions, stop others' sessions, manage nodes, manage team members, view audit log.
3. **Per-user auth tokens**: Each team member gets their own token (not shared). Relay maps token → user → team → permissions.
4. **Session ownership**: Sessions have an owner (the user who spawned them). Admins can see all sessions; members see only their own (configurable).
5. **Shared node pool**: Team's nodes are visible to all team members. Node affinity rules (e.g., "GPU node only for user X").
6. **Audit log**: Every action through the relay is logged: who spawned what, when, on which node, duration, exit code. Stored separately from session data. NOT encrypted (it's metadata).
7. **SSO/SAML**: Enterprise requirement. Integrate with Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace.
8. **Invitation flow**: Invite users by email, accept/decline, onboarding.

## Revenue model
- This is a Team/Enterprise tier feature, not available on Free/Pro individual plans
- Team ($99/mo base + $19/mo per seat): RBAC, shared namespace, audit log
- Enterprise (custom): SSO/SAML, compliance, dedicated support, custom roles

## Privacy implications with E2E encryption
- Audit log captures metadata only: who, when, which node, duration, exit code
- E2E encryption means admins cannot read others' prompts/results through the relay
- For "manager oversight" use case: need opt-in session sharing where user explicitly shares their session key with team admin
- Key management becomes more complex: team-level keys vs individual keys

## Implementation complexity
- High. User management, RBAC, invitation flows, SSO — this is standard SaaS plumbing but significant effort.
- Can be built incrementally: start with shared token (current), then per-user tokens, then RBAC.

## Moat analysis
Strong moat. Team features are hard to self-host:
- User management requires a separate auth system
- Audit logging requires centralized storage
- RBAC requires policy enforcement at the relay level
- SSO requires integration with identity providers

title: Mutual authentication for direct daemon connections
description:
Direct connections (LAN/Tailscale) need authentication equivalent to relay token auth.

Current state: relay uses --token for auth, E2E uses X25519 key exchange. Direct connections have neither.

Plan:
- Reuse existing E2E key infrastructure (X25519 keys at ~/.orka/keys/)
- On direct WS connect, client and daemon perform mutual key exchange
- Both sides verify the other's public key against known keys
- First connection: TOFU (trust on first use) with fingerprint display for manual verification
- Subsequent connections: reject if key changed (like SSH known_hosts)

Storage:
- ~/.orka/keys/known_nodes.json — maps node-id to public key fingerprint
- On first connect to new node: prompt user to accept fingerprint
- `orka trust <node-id>` to manually trust
- `orka untrust <node-id>` to remove

Security properties:
- No plaintext session data on the wire, ever
- MITM protection via key pinning after first use
- Forward secrecy via ephemeral ECDH per connection (already in crypto.ts)

title: Mutual key exchange on direct WS connect
description:
On direct connection (not through relay), client and daemon perform X25519 key exchange using existing crypto.ts infrastructure. Both sides verify against known_nodes trust store. Reject if key mismatch (like SSH known_hosts).

Implementation:
- Extend WS handshake for direct connections:
  1. Client connects to daemon WS endpoint
  2. Client sends 'auth.hello' message with client public key
  3. Daemon responds with 'auth.challenge' containing daemon public key + nonce
  4. Client verifies daemon pubkey against trust store
  5. If new node (TOFU): display fingerprint, prompt user to accept
  6. If known node with matching key: proceed
  7. If known node with DIFFERENT key: abort with key_mismatch error
  8. Client sends 'auth.response' with signed nonce (proves client identity)
  9. Daemon verifies client against its own trust store
  10. Shared secret derived via X25519 ECDH (reuse crypto.ts deriveSharedKey)
- All subsequent messages encrypted with derived AES-256-GCM key
- Server-side: packages/daemon/src/server.ts — handle auth handshake
- Client-side: packages/daemon/src/remote-client.ts — initiate auth handshake

Files: packages/daemon/src/server.ts, packages/daemon/src/remote-client.ts

title: Key change detection and SSH-style warning
description:

Implementation:
- In the mutual auth handshake, when trust store returns 'key_mismatch':
  - Print bold/red warning banner (similar to SSH):
    @@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@
    @    WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED!    @
    @@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@
  - Show: node-id, expected fingerprint, received fingerprint
  - Explain: 'Someone could be eavesdropping on you right now (man-in-the-middle attack)!'
  - Instruct: 'To accept the new key, run: orka trust --force <node-id>'
  - Abort the connection (exit code 1)

title: RTT-based optimal path selection (direct vs relay)
description:
When multiple paths exist to a daemon node, the client should pick the fastest one.

Scenario: user has a daemon at home. Paths available:
1. Direct LAN (if on same network) — ~1ms RTT
2. Tailscale direct (if both in tailnet) — ~5-20ms RTT
3. Via cloud relay — ~50-200ms RTT

Behavior:
- On connect, client probes all known paths to the target node in parallel
- Pick the path with lowest RTT
- If the active path degrades (RTT spikes, disconnects), failover to next-best path
- Seamless reconnect: in-flight RPC requests are retried on the new path

Implementation:
- Client maintains a ranked list of endpoints per node
- Endpoints come from: discovery (mDNS), relay node list, manual config, cached history
- Periodic RTT probing (ping/pong on WS) to detect path quality changes
- `orka status` shows current path, RTT, and alternatives

Config:
```toml
[network]
prefer_direct = true       # try direct before relay
probe_interval = 30        # seconds between RTT probes
failover_threshold = 500   # ms RTT to trigger failover
```

title: Parallel RTT probing
description:
On connect, probe all known endpoints for target node in parallel. Use WS ping/pong or a lightweight 'ping' RPC method. Pick lowest RTT. Periodic re-probe every [network] probe_interval seconds (default 30).

Implementation:
- On connect to a node: query endpoint registry for all known endpoints
- Probe all endpoints in parallel using Promise.allSettled():
  - Open temporary WS connection to each endpoint
  - Send ping RPC and measure round-trip time
  - Close temporary connections (except the winner)
- Select endpoint with lowest RTT, connect RemoteClient to it
- Periodic re-probe (setInterval, .unref()):
  - Every probe_interval seconds, probe alternative endpoints
  - If a significantly faster endpoint is found (>50% improvement), log it but don't auto-switch (that's the failover task)
  - Update RTT values in endpoint registry
- New RPC method on daemon: 'ping' — returns immediately with {pong: true, timestamp}

title: Automatic failover on path degradation
description:
Monitor active connection RTT. If RTT exceeds [network] failover_threshold (default 500ms) for 3 consecutive probes, transparently reconnect to next-best endpoint. Retry in-flight RPCs on new connection.

Implementation:
- RTT monitoring: track RTT of each RPC response on the active connection
- Degradation detection: if 3 consecutive RTT measurements exceed failover_threshold:
  - Log warning: 'Path degradation detected: RTT {avg}ms > {threshold}ms'
  - Trigger failover sequence
- Failover sequence:
  1. Select next-best endpoint from registry (by lastRtt)
  2. Open new WS connection to that endpoint
  3. Perform auth handshake on new connection
  4. Collect in-flight RPC request IDs from old connection
  5. Re-send in-flight RPCs on new connection
  6. Close old connection gracefully
  7. Update endpoint registry with new RTT values
- Idempotency: RPCs must be safe to retry (they already are — JSON-RPC is stateless)
- Config: [network] failover_threshold = 500, failover_consecutive = 3
- Guard: don't failover more than once per 30s to avoid flapping

Allow propagating Claude Code / Codex provider configuration from a central control point to all remote nodes.

## Use cases
1. Push .claude/settings.json (permissions, hooks, MCP servers) to all nodes
2. Push codex config to all nodes
3. Override per-node where needed
4. Opt-in — nodes can accept or reject pushed config

## Critical: config layering and merge semantics
Must deeply analyze how each provider handles configuration layering:

**Claude Code:**
- Project-level: .claude/settings.json, CLAUDE.md, .cursorrules
- User-level: ~/.claude/settings.json
- Session-level: CLI flags, env vars
- How do these layers merge? Which wins? Can we inject without clobbering?

**Codex:**
- Project-level: codex.json, .codex/
- User-level: ~/.codex/
- Session-level: CLI flags
- Same questions about merge semantics

**Key requirements:**
- Research exactly WHERE we can inject config for each provider (env vars? settings files? CLI flags? wrapper scripts?)
- Ensure our injected config does NOT overwrite user's local project config unless explicitly requested
- Support merge modes: 'merge' (deep merge, local wins), 'override' (remote wins), 'append' (add without removing)
- Per-setting granularity where possible (e.g. push hooks but keep local MCP servers)
- Dry-run mode: show what WOULD change before applying
- Rollback: ability to undo a pushed config

## Architecture
- Relay API for config distribution
- Daemon endpoint to accept + apply config with merge semantics
- CLI: orka config push [--all | --node <id>] [--mode merge|override] [--dry-run]
- Dashboard UI for config management and diff preview

Ties into vault encrypted config storage and config architecture (orka-jjdr).

title: Codex sandbox blocks bun install: tmpdir + network

Codex sandbox blocks bun install in worktrees two ways:

1. **Tmpdir write denied** — bun needs to write to a temp directory during install. Even TMPDIR=/tmp doesn't help.
2. **Network access blocked** — sandbox blocks outbound network, so bun can't download packages at all.

Agents waste tokens hacking around this (creating zustand shims, symlinking node_modules, etc.)

## Potential solutions:
- **Pre-install dependencies**: run `bun install` in the worktree BEFORE spawning the codex agent (in orchestrator.ts after worktreeCreate). This avoids both problems since orka itself isn't sandboxed.
- **Symlink node_modules**: symlink worktree/node_modules → main repo node_modules after worktree creation. Bun resolves workspace deps from there.
- **Configure codex sandbox**: investigate if codex has network/tmpdir permissions config
- **Use --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox**: nuclear option, skip sandbox entirely

Recommended: symlink node_modules in orchestrator.ts right after worktreeCreate(). Cheapest fix, no network needed.

title: SaaS: Managed compute nodes
description:
We run daemon nodes on beefy machines so users can offload agent sessions to cloud compute.

## What it is
Users spawn sessions that run on our managed infrastructure instead of their own machines. We provide pre-configured nodes with Claude CLI, Codex, aider, tmux, git — ready to go. Users push their repo (or we clone from GitHub), and the agent runs in an isolated environment.

## Architecture changes needed
1. **Node provisioning**: Spin up daemon instances on demand (Fly.io, Railway, or bare EC2/Hetzner). Each user gets isolated compute via containers or VMs.
2. **Repo sync**: Users need their code on our nodes. Options: (a) git clone from user's remote (needs deploy key), (b) rsync/push from CLI, (c) mount via NFS/FUSE. Git clone is simplest — user provides repo URL + auth.
3. **Result retrieval**: After session completes, user needs the diff/branch. Options: (a) push to user's remote (needs write access), (b) download patch via relay, (c) `orka diff` and `orka merge` already work over RPC.
4. **Ephemeral vs persistent nodes**: Ephemeral (spin up per session, tear down after) is simpler and more secure. Persistent nodes are cheaper for heavy users.
5. **Secret management**: Agent sessions need API keys (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, etc.). Users provide via encrypted config, stored in our vault, injected at runtime. With E2E encryption, we could have users encrypt secrets with the node's public key.
6. **Isolation**: Each session runs in its own container. No cross-user data leakage.
7. **GPU support**: For codex or other GPU-accelerated backends.

## Revenue model
- **Pay-per-session**: $0.05/session + $0.01/min compute time (covers infra cost + margin)
- **Compute credits**: Buy credits in bulk at discount ($50 = 1200 credits, $200 = 5500 credits)
- **Reserved nodes**: $149/mo for a dedicated always-on node (for teams that need instant startup)
- **GPU tier**: Premium pricing for GPU-equipped nodes

## Privacy implications with E2E encryption
- With E2E: We cannot read the prompts, code, or results flowing through the relay
- WITHOUT E2E on the node itself: Our managed node DOES have access to the code and prompts (it must, to run the agent). This is the key tension.
- Mitigation: Confidential computing (AMD SEV, Intel TDX), attestation, minimal logging, SOC2 compliance
- Alternative: "Bring your own key" for the LLM API — user provides their Anthropic key, we never see it (injected via encrypted secret)

## Implementation complexity
- High. Requires container orchestration, secret management, repo sync, billing integration, isolation guarantees.
- This is the highest-revenue but highest-effort item.

## Moat analysis
Strong moat: users don't want to manage machines. Especially compelling for:
- Teams without spare machines
- CI/CD integration (spawn agents from GitHub Actions)
- Burst capacity (10 agents in parallel during crunch time)

title: Fix: codex agents can't git commit in sandbox mode

Codex sandbox blocks 3 operations even with --sandbox danger-full-access:

1. **git commit** — `.git/worktrees/sess-*/index.lock` is at `/home/user/prj/orka/.git/worktrees/` which is OUTSIDE the worktree's writable root (`~/.orka/worktrees/sess-*`). Sandbox only allows writes inside --cd path.

2. **bun install** — `bun is unable to write files to tempdir: AccessDenied` — sandbox blocks tempdir writes.

3. **rm command** — sandbox policy rejects `rm`, agents had to use `unlink` workaround.

## Potential fixes (pick one or combine):
- **Option A**: Use `--cd /home/user/prj/orka` so sandbox includes .git/ in writable scope, but then agent works in main repo not worktree
- **Option B**: Set TMPDIR=/tmp in session env to fix bun install
- **Option C**: Use full git clones instead of worktrees — .git/ lives inside working dir
- **Option D**: Post-session auto-commit hook in orka daemon — if session exits with uncommitted changes, auto-commit before merge
- **Option E**: Investigate codex --sandbox danger-full-access docs more carefully, maybe there's a way to add extra writable paths

title: Configurable post_create hook for worktrees
description:
Generic worktree lifecycle hooks — user-configurable scripts that run at different stages of session lifecycle. Orka MUST NOT hardcode any project-specific behavior (no bun install, no npm ci, etc.).

## Hook stages:
- `post_create` — after worktree created, BEFORE agent starts. Runs outside sandbox with full access. This is where users solve dependency installation.
- `pre_agent` — right before agent process spawns
- `post_agent` — after agent process exits (before reap/cleanup)
- `pre_merge` — before merging worktree back (e.g. run tests/lint to validate)

## Configuration layers (higher overrides lower):
1. CLI flags: `orka spawn --hook post_create='bun install'`
2. Project config: `.orka.toml` in project root
3. Global config: `~/.orka/config.toml`

## Example configs:

```toml
# .orka.toml (JS project)
[hooks]
post_create = "bun install"
pre_merge = "bun test"

# .orka.toml (Python project)  
[hooks]
post_create = "pip install -r requirements.txt"
pre_merge = "pytest"

# .orka.toml (Rust project)
[hooks]
post_create = "cargo fetch"
pre_merge = "cargo test"
```

## Implementation:
- Parse .orka.toml from projectPath during spawn
- Merge with global config hooks
- Execute hooks in orchestrator.ts at the right lifecycle points
- Pass environment: ORKA_SESSION_ID, ORKA_WORKTREE_PATH, ORKA_PROJECT_PATH
- Log hook output to session log
- Fail spawn if post_create hook fails (non-zero exit)

This replaces orka-k74 (symlink node_modules) and orka-9ln (bun install fix) with a proper generic solution.

title: SaaS: LLM API key management and cost aggregation
description:
Manage LLM API keys centrally, aggregate costs across all sessions, set budgets and alerts.

## What it is
Instead of each developer managing their own Anthropic/OpenAI API keys, the team admin configures keys centrally. Orka injects them into sessions and tracks total spend across all users and sessions. Budgets can be set per-user, per-project, or team-wide.

## Architecture changes needed
1. **Key vault**: Encrypted storage for API keys. Keys are per-team, optionally per-project. Injected into session environment at spawn time.
2. **Cost aggregation**: Parse session results (already done by result-parser.ts — costUsd, tokens) and aggregate across team. Store in analytics DB.
3. **Budget enforcement**: Before spawning a session, check if user/project/team has exceeded budget. Reject spawn if over budget.
4. **Budget alerts**: Email/Slack/webhook when spend reaches 80%, 100% of budget.
5. **Cost allocation**: Tag sessions with project/team/purpose, generate cost reports per dimension.

## Revenue model
- Bundled with Team tier ($99/mo) — key management, cost dashboard, budget alerts
- Enterprise: advanced cost allocation, chargeback reports, integration with finance tools

## Privacy implications
- API keys are the most sensitive data. Must be encrypted at rest and in transit.
- With managed nodes: we inject keys into the environment, so we technically have access (but can use secure enclaves).
- With user's own nodes: keys can be stored locally, never sent to relay. Only cost metadata reported.
- E2E encryption protects keys in transit through relay.

## Implementation complexity
- Medium. Key storage and injection is straightforward. Budget enforcement is relay-side middleware.
- Cost aggregation builds on existing result-parser.ts infrastructure.

title: Agent session supervision — detect and handle hung/stalled agents
description:
Agent sess-ef13a1c7 completed its work (wrote 402-line research doc) but hung for 1+ hour without committing or exiting. The orchestrator had no way to detect this stall.

## Problem
- Agent finished meaningful work but got stuck (likely on beads hook, git commit, or infinite loop)
- No timeout or heartbeat detection
- User had to manually notice and investigate
- All output was lost until manual intervention

## Evidence from this incident
- Session running for 1h12m, process alive, CPU 5%
- Logs showed all research done, doc written to disk
- Git status: doc untracked (never committed)
- Likely cause: beads Dolt hook blocking git commit, or agent stuck in write/retry loop

## Supervision features needed

### 1. Activity timeout
- Track last event timestamp per session
- If no new events for N minutes (configurable, default 10?), flag as stalled
- Different from idle timer (idle = turn completed, stalled = mid-turn no progress)

### 2. Heartbeat detection
- Expect regular events from running sessions (content.delta, tool calls, etc.)
- No events for extended period → stall warning

### 3. Stall response options
- Warn in dashboard: 'Session appears stalled — no activity for 10m'
- Auto-send nudge message: 'Are you stuck? Please commit your work and continue.'
- Auto-stop after extended stall (configurable)
- Preserve work: before killing, capture git status, diff, last events

### 4. Dashboard indicators
- Show time since last event on running sessions
- Amber warning after N minutes of no activity
- Red after M minutes

### 5. CLI
- orka ps shows stall warning
- orka logs shows last activity timestamp

### 6. Integration with existing features
- Idle timer: different — idle is after turn.completed, stall is during turn
- Rate limit detection: different — rate_limit_event is explicit, stall is implicit
- Follow-up messages: could be used as nudge mechanism

## Supervision modes (future)
- Passive: just detect and warn
- Active: auto-nudge stalled agents
- Aggressive: auto-kill after timeout, preserve work

title: Graceful connection draining on SIGTERM
description:
On SIGTERM: stop accepting new connections, finish in-flight RPCs (30s timeout), then close. Use WS close frame with 'going_away' code (1001).

Implementation:
- Listen for SIGTERM/SIGINT in relay server
- Set a 'draining' flag to reject new WS upgrades (respond 503)
- For each active WS connection: wait for in-flight RPC responses (track pending request IDs)
- After 30s hard timeout, force-close remaining connections with code 1001 ('going_away')
- Exit cleanly after all connections closed or timeout

Test: relay restart doesn't drop active requests — client should see the response for any RPC that was in-flight when SIGTERM arrived.

title: SaaS: Priority scheduling and queue management
description:
Paid tiers get priority node selection and queue management for burst workloads.

## What it is
When multiple users share nodes (managed or marketplace), paid users get priority. Also: queue management for burst workloads — spawn 50 sessions, they queue and execute as nodes become available, with priority users going first.

## Architecture changes needed
1. **Queue in relay**: Currently the relay routes immediately or fails (503 if no nodes). Add a queue: if all nodes are busy, enqueue the request. Process queue FIFO with priority weighting.
2. **Priority tiers**: Free = lowest priority, Pro = medium, Team/Enterprise = highest. Within same tier, FIFO.
3. **Node capacity tracking**: Relay tracks how many sessions each node can handle concurrently (already has activeRequests). Add maxConcurrent per node registration.
4. **Queue status API**: Users can check queue position via `orka ps --queued` or API.
5. **Auto-scaling trigger**: When queue depth exceeds threshold, spin up more managed nodes (if user is on managed compute plan).

## Revenue model
- Bundled with paid tiers (Pro/Team/Enterprise get priority)
- Burst capacity add-on: $49/mo for auto-scaling managed nodes during queue pressure
- Queue skip: pay-per-use $0.10 to jump to front of queue (controversial but effective)

## Privacy implications
- Minimal. Queue management only sees metadata: session ID, user ID, priority tier, node capacity.
- E2E encryption unaffected — queued messages are encrypted blobs waiting to be forwarded.

## Implementation complexity
- Medium. Requires adding a queue to the relay, priority logic, capacity tracking.
- Natural extension of the existing relay architecture.

title: SaaS: Relay-as-a-Service (hosted relay)
description:
Hosted multi-tenant relay so users don't need to run their own infrastructure.

## What it is
A managed relay instance (relay.orka.dev) that users point their CLI and daemon nodes at. Users get an account, an auth token, and a relay URL. Their nodes register with our relay, and their CLI connects through it.

## Architecture changes needed
1. **Multi-tenant relay**: Current relay uses a single shared token. Needs per-account auth tokens, account isolation (nodes only visible to their owner), and account-scoped node routing.
2. **Account/token management**: REST API + dashboard for signup, API key generation, token rotation. Store in Postgres/Turso.
3. **Usage metering**: Track per-account: WS connections, messages relayed, bandwidth, connected nodes, concurrent sessions. The relay already parses only `node` and `id` from envelopes — meter at this level.
4. **Rate limiting**: Per-account rate limits on connections and messages/sec.
5. **High availability**: Multiple relay instances behind a load balancer. Stateless relay design (nodes register to specific instance, need sticky sessions or shared node registry via Redis/NATS).
6. **TLS termination**: wss:// endpoints with Let's Encrypt.
7. **Geographic distribution**: Relay instances in multiple regions for low latency.

## Revenue model
- **Free tier**: 1 node, 100 sessions/month, single user
- **Pro** ($29/mo): 5 nodes, unlimited sessions, priority support
- **Team** ($99/mo): 20 nodes, team management, RBAC, audit logs
- **Enterprise** (custom): Unlimited nodes, SLA, dedicated relay instance, SSO

## Privacy implications with E2E encryption
- Relay sees: envelope metadata (node ID, request ID, method name if not encrypted), connection timing, message sizes, IP addresses
- Relay CANNOT see: params, results, prompts, code, diffs — all encrypted end-to-end
- This is a strong selling point: "we literally cannot read your code"

## Implementation complexity
- Medium. The relay is already built and transparent. Main work is multi-tenancy, auth, metering, and ops.
- Depends on: E2E encryption (orka-vt0) for the privacy story

## Moat analysis
Self-hosting a relay is easy (it's a single `orka relay` command). The moat is:
- Convenience (zero ops)
- Uptime/SLA guarantees
- Geographic distribution
- Team features layered on top

title: Pairing flow: client-side + Noise verification
description:
Implement full client-side pairing flow per spec §1.5 + §1.6.

Flow:
1. Parse pairing code → extract secret
2. Derive enroll_id from secret via BLAKE3
3. Connect to relay: wss://relay/v1/pair/<enroll_id>
4. Send pair_client_hello
5. Receive pair_server_hello → validate version, suite
6. Compute pair_context, pair_aad
7. Compute SPAKE2 client side (pA), send pair_init
8. Receive pair_resp (pB)
9. Derive Ke, Ka, KcA, KcB
10. Compute + send pair_confirm1
11. Receive pair_confirm2 → verify server MAC
12. Derive boot keys, decrypt pair_bootstrap → extract node info

**Critical §1.6 — client commit only after Noise verification:**
13. Close pairing session
14. Open transport connection to node_paths[0]
15. Perform real Noise_NK handshake with received noise_static_pubkey
16. Only after successful Noise handshake: save node to config
17. Send pair_done to node via the verified transport

title: Support custom config directories / profiles for all backends

Allow users to specify which config directory, authentication, and profile to use for spawned agents. Tied to workspaces — each workspace can have a default profile.

- User has work and personal Claude Code accounts (different API keys, different orgs)
- User wants workspace A to always use work credentials, workspace B to use personal
- Currently no way to propagate auth context into spawned agents
- Same applies to Codex (different OpenAI orgs/keys)

## Profiles system
Profiles bundle together: auth credentials, config dirs, backend settings, and can be bound to workspaces.

```toml
[profiles.work]
backends.claude-code.config_dir = "~/.claude-work"
backends.claude-code.api_key_env = "ANTHROPIC_API_KEY_WORK"
backends.codex.profile = "work"
backends.codex.api_key_env = "OPENAI_API_KEY_WORK"

[profiles.personal]
backends.claude-code.config_dir = "~/.claude-personal"
backends.codex.profile = "personal"

[workspaces.my-company-repo]
profile = "work"

[workspaces.side-project]
profile = "personal"
```

## Auth propagation
- **Claude Code**: CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR env var (controls which account/org is used), ANTHROPIC_API_KEY override
- **Codex**: --profile flag, OPENAI_API_KEY override
- **API keys**: stored securely — either in vault (orka encrypted storage) or referenced via env var names
- **Never store raw API keys in config.toml** — use env var references or vault

## Features
1. `orka spawn --profile work` — explicit profile selection
2. Workspace default profile — auto-selects based on project path
3. Profile inheritance — workspace profile overrides default, CLI flag overrides workspace
4. Dashboard: profile selector in spawn dialog
5. Fleet propagation — push profiles to remote nodes (via vault encrypted storage)
6. `orka profile list` — show configured profiles
7. `orka profile test <name>` — verify auth works (try claude --version, codex --version with profile env)

## Implementation
- Claude Code: set CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR + optional ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in spawn env
- Codex: pass --profile or set OPENAI_API_KEY in spawn env
- Store profile name in session record for retry reproducibility
- Adapter receives profile config and injects appropriate env vars

## Security
- API keys referenced by env var name, not stored in config
- Vault integration for secure key storage across fleet
- Profile env vars never logged or exposed in API responses (same as current env redaction)

- No in-session rekey

title: Use bun build --compile for daemon Docker image

FROM debian:trixie-slim

title: Harden TypeScript config and add agent-agnostic lint hooks
description:
## Current State
- `tsconfig.json`: only `strict: true`, missing all extra strict flags
- ESLint: completely absent (no config, no dependencies)
- Hooks: none configured (no husky, no .githooks, no claude code hooks)

## Goal
Make coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, any future agent) trip over type errors and lint violations before they can produce sloppy code. Agent-agnostic enforcement.

## Scope

### 1. Harden tsconfig.json (root + per-package)
Add to root tsconfig.json:
- `noUncheckedIndexedAccess: true`
- `exactOptionalPropertyTypes: true`
- `noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature: true`
- `noImplicitOverride: true`
- `noImplicitReturns: true`
- `noUnusedLocals: true`
- `noUnusedParameters: true`
- `noFallthroughCasesInSwitch: true`
- `useUnknownInCatchVariables: true` (already in strict, but explicit)
- `strictBuiltinIteratorReturn: true`
- `verbatimModuleSyntax: true`
- `isolatedModules: true`
- `moduleDetection: "force"`
- `noEmit: true`

Dashboard tsconfig may need separate treatment (React/JSX, DOM libs).

### 2. Add ESLint with typescript-eslint strict type-checked
- Install deps: `eslint`, `@eslint/js`, `typescript-eslint`
- Create `eslint.config.mjs` with flat config
- Use `recommendedTypeChecked` + `strictTypeChecked` presets
- `projectService: true` for type-aware linting
- Explicit error rules:
  - `no-explicit-any`, `no-unsafe-*` (assignment/argument/call/member-access/return/type-assertion)
  - `ban-ts-comment` (ts-ignore/ts-nocheck banned, ts-expect-error requires 10+ char description)
  - `no-non-null-assertion`, `no-empty-object-type`, `no-unsafe-function-type`, `no-wrapper-object-types`
  - `no-unnecessary-condition`, `restrict-template-expressions`
  - `no-restricted-syntax` AST selectors to ban `as any`, `<any>`, double assertions (`as unknown as X`)

### 3. Add package.json scripts
- `"lint": "eslint ."` 
- `"typecheck": "tsc --build"`
- `"check": "bun run typecheck && bun run lint"`

### 4. Agent config layout: `docs/agents/` as single source of truth
Agent-specific hook configs and docs live in `docs/agents/`. Files that agent tools expect at specific paths should be **symlinks** pointing into `docs/agents/`.

Example:
```
docs/agents/
  claude-settings.json   # Claude Code settings with hooks
  AGENTS.md              # agent workflow conventions
  ...

.claude/settings.json -> ../docs/agents/claude-settings.json
AGENTS.md -> docs/agents/AGENTS.md
```

### 5. Set up hooks

**Git pre-commit hook** (`.githooks/pre-commit`): runs `tsc --build --noEmit` and `eslint` on staged files. Simple shell script, no husky dependency. Enable via `git config core.hooksPath .githooks`. Fires for ANY tool that commits — fully agent-agnostic.

**Claude Code hooks** (`docs/agents/claude-settings.json`, symlinked to `.claude/settings.json`): PreToolUse hook on Edit/Write that runs lint on changed files, giving Claude Code inline feedback during editing.

### 6. Fix existing code
After enabling strict config + ESLint, fix all existing violations. This will likely be the bulk of the work — expect `as any`, untyped catches, unchecked index access, etc. throughout the codebase.

## References
- TS strict flags: https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig/strict.html
- typescript-eslint getting started: https://typescript-eslint.io/getting-started/
- Avoiding anys: https://typescript-eslint.io/blog/avoiding-anys/
- projectService: https://typescript-eslint.io/packages/parser

title: Graceful handling of transient API errors (529/500/503) with auto-retry
description:
When provider APIs return transient errors or subscription token limits are exhausted, sessions need graceful handling with auto-retry and auto-continue.

## Verified findings from experiments (docs/api-error-experiments.md)

### Claude Code behavior
- **Retries internally** — up to 10 times with exponential backoff for ALL errors (including 401!)
- **`system.api_retry` events** visible in stream-json mode — we currently IGNORE these in mapClaudeEvent()
- **`rate_limit_event`** emitted with rich info:
  - `status`: 'allowed' | 'allowed_warning' | 'rejected'
  - `rateLimitType`: 'five_hour' | 'seven_day'
  - `utilization`: 0.0-1.0 (how much of limit used)
  - `surpassedThreshold`: 0.75, 0.9 warning levels
  - `resetsAt`: unix timestamp of limit reset
  - `overageStatus`: 'rejected', `overageDisabledReason`: 'out_of_credits'
- **Stderr is empty** — all error info comes through stdout stream-json events
- **No API key → still works** via account defaults on subscription

### Codex behavior
- **Does NOT retry** — immediately emits error + turn/completed(failed)
- Structured error info in `codexErrorInfo`

## What to implement

### Phase 1: Capture existing events we're ignoring
- Map `system.api_retry` events in claude adapter → show in dashboard/CLI
- Map `rate_limit_event` events → show utilization warnings in dashboard
- Dashboard: show rate limit bar (utilization %, resets at time)

### Phase 2: Token limit exhaustion → auto-continue
- When `rate_limit_event` has `status: 'rejected'` or Claude exits due to limit:
  - Set session to 'waiting_for_limit' or 'rate_limited' status
  - Show in dashboard: 'Rate limited — resets at 15:00 (2h 30m)'
  - Auto-schedule resumeSession() at `resetsAt` timestamp
  - User can also manually continue earlier if limits reset
- For Codex: detect rate limit errors, schedule retry with backoff

### Phase 3: Transient error retry (for Codex primarily)
- Claude handles retries internally — we just need to surface the events
- Codex needs our orchestrator-level retry with exponential backoff
- Error classification: transient (529/500/503/429) vs fatal (401/403/400)
- Config: [retry] section in config.toml

### Phase 4: UI polish
- Dashboard: rate limit utilization bar in session header or sidebar
- Dashboard: 'Retrying...' / 'Rate limited until...' states
- Dashboard: countdown to limit reset
- CLI: orka ps shows rate limit info
- CLI: orka attach shows retry/rate limit events

## Key insight
Claude Code already retries API errors internally. Our main job is to:
1. Surface the retry/rate_limit events we're currently ignoring
2. Handle the case where the limit is fully exhausted and the process exits
3. Auto-resume when the limit resets

title: SaaS: Node marketplace (community compute)
description:
Users contribute spare compute capacity, others pay to use it. Orka takes a cut.

## What it is
A marketplace where users with idle machines register them as available nodes. Other users can spawn sessions on these community nodes. Orka handles matchmaking, billing, and trust.

## Architecture changes needed
1. **Node listing/discovery**: Providers register nodes with specs (CPU, RAM, GPU, region, availability hours). Stored in relay's DB.
2. **Pricing**: Providers set their own rates (e.g., $0.02/min). Orka takes 20% platform fee.
3. **Billing/escrow**: Users pre-pay or have a balance. Sessions are metered. Provider gets paid after session completes successfully.
4. **Trust/reputation**: Rating system for nodes (uptime, success rate, speed). Users can filter by rating.
5. **Isolation**: Critical — users' code runs on strangers' machines. Requires: container isolation, network sandboxing, ephemeral workdirs, no persistent state after session.
6. **E2E encryption**: Essential for marketplace. Users must trust that node operators cannot read their code. But the node MUST decrypt to run the agent. This is the fundamental tension.
7. **Attestation**: Confidential computing or remote attestation to prove the node is running unmodified Orka daemon in a secure enclave.

## Revenue model
- Platform fee: 20% of session cost
- Featured listings: Providers pay to be listed first
- Guaranteed availability: Providers stake a deposit, get higher rates

## Privacy implications
- CRITICAL RISK: Node operators have access to decrypted code/prompts (the agent must read the code to work on it)
- E2E encryption protects transit but not execution
- Mitigations: Confidential computing, legal agreements, reputation system, insurance
- This is the hardest privacy problem in the entire SaaS

## Implementation complexity
- Very high. Billing, trust, isolation, dispute resolution, fraud prevention.
- Likely Phase 3+ — after relay-as-a-service and managed compute are proven.

## Moat analysis
Very strong moat if achieved — network effects (more providers = better availability = more users = more providers). But extremely hard to bootstrap and fraught with security risks.

2. **User level** — per-user overrides

Key questions to resolve:
- How should agents receive context/instructions? (e.g. system prompt additions, env vars, config files copied into worktree)
- How should backend-specific settings be configured? (sandbox mode, extra CLI flags, model defaults)
- How should worktree lifecycle hooks be configured at each level?
- How do configs merge/override across levels? (node < user < repo precedence)
- Should there be a way to inject pre/post prompt text per-backend per-project?
- How should proactive error diagnostics and suggested fixes be configured?

This replaces the removed CODEX_NO_BEADS hardcoded instruction and the ad-hoc approach to backend customization. Related issues: orka-bt3 (hooks), orka-gfl (custom config dirs), orka-iqk (agent session customization), orka-rxl (proactive diagnostics).

title: SaaS: Multi-tenant relay auth and account system
description:
Foundation for all SaaS features: multi-tenant auth, account management, API keys, billing integration.

## What it is
The core infrastructure that all paid features depend on. Currently the relay uses a single shared token. This replaces it with proper multi-tenant auth: accounts, API keys, usage tracking, Stripe billing.

## Architecture changes needed
1. **Account model**: accounts table (id, email, name, plan, stripe_customer_id, created_at)
2. **API key management**: api_keys table (id, account_id, key_hash, name, scopes, created_at, last_used_at, revoked_at). Keys are bcrypt-hashed, displayed once at creation.
3. **Relay auth middleware**: Replace single-token check with API key lookup. Extract account from key, attach to request context.
4. **Account-scoped node isolation**: Nodes register with an API key. Relay maps node → account. Client requests only route to nodes owned by the same account (or shared via team).
5. **Usage metering**: Per-account counters: sessions_this_month, nodes_connected, messages_relayed. Stored in Postgres or Redis.
6. **Stripe integration**: Subscription management, usage-based billing, invoices. Webhook handler for payment events.
7. **Account dashboard**: Web app for account settings, API key management, usage view, billing.

## Revenue model
- This IS the billing system. Required for all paid features.
- Free tier: auto-created on signup, limited usage
- Upgrade flow: Stripe Checkout → Pro/Team/Enterprise

## Implementation complexity
- High but well-understood. Standard SaaS plumbing.
- MUST be built before any paid features can ship.
- Suggested order: (1) Account model + API keys, (2) Relay auth, (3) Usage metering, (4) Stripe, (5) Dashboard

## Dependencies
- Blocks: all other SaaS features
- Depends on: nothing (can start immediately)

title: Fix beads/Dolt in agent worktrees — Dolt server not found
description:
Beads fails in agent worktrees because each worktree gets its own independent Dolt SQL server with an empty database.

## Root cause

- Worktree gets fresh .beads/dolt/ (empty DB)
- New Dolt server starts on ephemeral port for that empty DB
- All bd commands fail: 'database orka not found'

## IMPORTANT: No hardcoding in orka
Beads is just a project tool like any other. Orka must NOT have beads-specific code. The fix must use GENERIC configuration mechanisms that work for any project tool.

## Generic solutions (no beads-specific code)

### Option A: .orka.env file (simplest)
- Orka reads .orka.env from project root before spawn
- User adds: BEADS_DOLT_HOST=127.0.0.1 and reads port dynamically
- Generic — works for any tool that needs env vars in agent sessions

### Option B: Pre-spawn hook in .orka.toml
- [hooks] before_spawn = 'script that exports env vars'
- Script reads .beads/dolt-server.port and sets BEADS_DOLT_PORT
- Generic — user writes whatever hook they need

### Option C: Workspace env settings
- Workspace entity already supports settings
- Add env vars to workspace settings in dashboard
- Propagated to all sessions in that workspace

### Option D: env section in .orka.toml
- [env] section with key=value pairs, sourced before spawn
- Supports dynamic values via shell expansion
- Generic — any project uses this for any tool

## Recommendation
Option D (.orka.toml [env] section) is the most natural. Already planned in orka-jjdr (config architecture). This unblocks beads and any similar tool (Docker env, cloud credentials, etc.)

## Depends on
- orka-jjdr: Config architecture (env propagation feature)

title: In-place session mode — run agent without creating a worktree

Currently all sessions create a git worktree. Some use cases don't need one:

## Use cases
1. **Supervisor sessions** — orchestrate other agents, don't write code directly
2. **Read-only analysis** — audit, review, research tasks that only read the codebase
3. **Quick one-off tasks** — simple questions, file lookups, no code changes expected
4. **Non-git projects** — directories that aren't git repos

## Proposed behavior
- `orka spawn --no-worktree` or `orka spawn --in-place`
- Agent runs directly in the project directory (cwd = projectPath)
- No branch creation, no worktree setup/cleanup overhead
- Faster startup (skip worktree creation which can be slow for large repos)
- Still gets a session record, events, logs — everything except worktree isolation

## Considerations
- Risk: agent modifies files in the main repo directly — user must be aware
- Permission mode interaction: supervised mode is extra important here
- Diff tracking: `orka diff` would show unstaged changes in the project dir, not isolated worktree
- Checkpoints (orka-8uiw): how do per-turn checkpoints work without isolated worktree? Probably skip or use stash-based approach
- Multiple in-place sessions on same project: potential conflicts
- Dashboard should clearly indicate session is in-place (no merge needed, changes are live)

## Implementation
- Add `worktreeMode: 'isolated' | 'in-place'` to SpawnRequest
- Skip worktree creation in orchestrator when in-place
- Set cwd to projectPath directly
- Skip merge flow (changes are already in the project)
- Adjust cleanup — nothing to clean up for in-place sessions

title: LAN/Tailscale daemon discovery via mDNS/DNS-SD
description:
Daemon nodes advertise presence on the local network so clients can find them without manual --remote config.

Approach:
- Use mDNS (multicast DNS) / DNS-SD to advertise _orka._tcp service
- TXT record contains: node-id, public key fingerprint, protocol version
- Works on physical LAN and Tailscale MagicDNS (Tailscale forwards mDNS within the tailnet)
- Client runs discovery on startup or on explicit `orka discover` command
- Cache discovered nodes with TTL, re-probe periodically

Security:
- Only advertise node ID and public key fingerprint — no session data
- Discovery is unauthenticated (like AirDrop) — actual connection requires E2E key exchange
- Option to disable discovery: `[network] discoverable = false` in config.toml

Implementation:
- Use multicast-dns or dns-sd npm package, or raw UDP socket for minimal deps
- Daemon: advertise on startup, withdraw on shutdown
- CLI: `orka discover` lists found nodes with latency
- Config: `[network] discoverable = true` (daemon), `[network] auto_discover = true` (client)

[dashboard]
enabled = true        # serve dashboard (default: true in dev, false in headless)
dev = true            # use Vite dev server (default: auto-detect)
port = 5173           # Vite dev port (dev mode only)
dist_path = 'packages/dashboard/dist'  # static files path (prod mode)

title: Replay-based E2E tests from real session logs
description:
Build a test framework that replays real raw session logs (from ~/.orka/logs/*.raw.jsonl) against the adapter/consumer/orchestrator pipeline.

Why: The TestShellAdapter is a simplified shell process that can't fully model real Claude Code or Codex behavior (turn lifecycle, tool use, rate limits, hooks, approvals, multi-turn, interrupts). Raw logs from real sessions contain the exact event sequences that the system handles in production.

Approach:
1. Create a ReplayAdapter that reads .raw.jsonl files and emits the same events a real adapter would
2. Feed these into the consumer/orchestrator pipeline
3. Assert on session state transitions, orchestration events, timing
4. Can extract test fixtures from any production session — captures edge cases (rate limits, hooks, agent tasks, compaction, multi-turn) naturally

Insights from analyzing real logs:
- Claude Code event flow: user → system.hook_started/response → system.init → assistant(thinking) → assistant(tool_use) → system.task_started/progress → user(tool_result) → ... → result(success/error)
- The adapter maps: system.init → session.started + turn.started; result → turn.completed; process exit → session.exited
- Rate limit events, hook events, and task lifecycle events all appear mid-turn
- Multi-turn sessions have multiple result events separated by user input

Key test scenarios from real logs:
- Single-turn background session completing normally
- Multi-turn interactive session with sendTurn delivery
- Rate limit event mid-session with auto-resume
- Session with hook approvals (PreToolUse)
- Agent spawning sub-agents (Task events)
- Session compaction
- Session cancelled mid-turn
- Long idle → hibernation → resume

title: SaaS: Session analytics dashboard
description:
Aggregated metrics dashboard showing cost, duration, success rate, and usage patterns across all agent sessions.

## What it is
A web dashboard (app.orka.dev) where users see analytics for their agent sessions: total spend, session success rate, average duration, tokens consumed, cost trends over time, per-project breakdowns, per-backend comparisons.

## Architecture changes needed
1. **Metadata collection at relay**: The relay already sees envelope metadata. Add: timestamp of each request/response, message size, method name (if unencrypted), latency (response time - request time), node health/availability.
2. **Optional client-side telemetry**: CLI sends anonymized usage events (session started, session completed, duration, cost, backend, exit code) to analytics endpoint. This data is NOT encrypted — it's voluntarily reported by the CLI.
3. **Analytics storage**: Time-series DB (ClickHouse, TimescaleDB) or simple Postgres with rollups.
4. **Web dashboard**: React/Next.js app showing charts, tables, filters.
5. **API**: REST/GraphQL API for programmatic access to analytics (CI/CD integration, custom dashboards).
6. **Alerts**: Notify when: cost exceeds budget, session failure rate spikes, node goes offline.

## What we CAN see (even with E2E encryption)
- Session count, timing (start/end/duration)
- Backend type (claude-code, codex, aider, shell)
- Node ID used
- Exit code (success/failure)
- Message count and sizes (bandwidth)
- Cost data (if client voluntarily reports it via `orka result` metadata)

## What we CANNOT see with E2E encryption
- Prompts, code, diffs, results
- What the agent actually did
- File contents, repo structure

## Revenue model
- Free: Basic session counts and status for last 7 days
- Pro: Full analytics, 90-day retention, cost tracking, per-project breakdown
- Team: Team-wide analytics, per-user breakdown, budget alerts, export to CSV/API
- Enterprise: Unlimited retention, custom dashboards, SAML/SSO, compliance reports

## Implementation complexity
- Medium-low for relay-side metrics (timestamps, counts)
- Medium for voluntary client telemetry
- Medium for the dashboard itself
- This is a good "land and expand" feature — show value before asking for money

## Moat analysis
Moderate moat. Users could build their own dashboards from traces.jsonl (we already export OpenTelemetry). But:
- Convenience of hosted dashboard
- Cross-machine aggregation (only relay sees all nodes)
- Team features (who ran what, cost allocation)
- Historical trends over months

title: Reaper incorrectly marks running sessions as completed, leaves orphaned tmux

Evidence: 6 orphaned tmux sessions with claude processes still running 2h+ after being marked completed within 100ms of spawn.

1. Add grace period — don't reap sessions started <30s ago
2. Double-check with tmuxHas() before marking completed
3. Kill tmux session when reaping as safety net

title: Safe prune: dry-run default, minimum age, soft delete
description:
Redesign orka prune to prevent accidental data loss. Three safety mechanisms:

A) Dry-run by default — orka prune without --confirm/--force only shows what WOULD be deleted (session count, log files, worktrees, traces). Requires explicit --confirm or --force flag to actually execute deletion.

B) Minimum age threshold — reject dangerously low --age values (e.g. 1m). Set a sensible minimum (e.g. 1h or 1d) unless --force is used. Prevents accidental mass deletion of recent sessions.

C) Soft delete / graduated cleanup — ALL artifacts are protected by default:
  - Session DB records (metadata, status, prompt, timestamps, tags)
  - Log files (~/.orka/logs/<id>.log)
  - Script files (~/.orka/scripts/<id>.sh)
  - Trace data (~/.orka/traces.jsonl entries for the session)
  - Worktrees (~/.orka/worktrees/<id>)

Prune should default to cleaning NOTHING without --confirm. With --confirm it cleans only worktrees (the disk-heavy part). Separate flags for deeper cleanup:
  --purge-logs    — also delete log and script files
  --purge-db      — also delete session records from SQLite
  --purge-all     — delete everything (worktrees + logs + scripts + DB records)
Traces are never deleted by prune (append-only audit log).

Implementation touches:
- packages/core/src/service.ts PruneOptions — add confirm, purgeLogs, purgeDb flags
- packages/daemon/src/local-client.ts pruneSessions() — respect new flags, keep current dbDeleteSessions removal, add conditional log/script deletion
- packages/cli/src/index.ts pruneCmd — add --confirm/--force/--purge-logs/--purge-db/--purge-all flags, implement dry-run summary output
- Minimum age validation (reject <1h unless --force)
- Revert the current unconditional log/script deletion in pruneSessions — it should also be behind --purge-logs

title: Store raw provider output as JSONL, add backfill command
description:
Store raw provider I/O as JSONL files. Daemon owns writing, adapters provide raw streams.

## Architecture

### RawProviderLine type (core)
`{ direction: 'in' | 'out', data: string, ts: string }`

### Adapter contract changes
- Add `rawEvents: AsyncIterable<RawProviderLine>` to `ProviderSessionHandle` — second stream alongside `events`
- Adapters emit raw lines: 'out' for each stdout line (before parsing), 'in' for each stdin write (prompt, sendTurn)
- Add `replayRawLog(threadId, lines: RawProviderLine[]): AsyncIterable<ProviderRuntimeEvent>` to adapter — pure function for backfill

### Daemon (consumer.ts)
- In `consumeProviderEvents()`, consume `handle.rawEvents` in parallel, write each to `~/.orka/logs/<session-id>.raw.jsonl`
- Each JSONL line: `{"ts":"...","dir":"in"|"out","data":"..."}`

### Per adapter
- Claude: each JSON line from stdout → dir:out, each stdin write → dir:in
- Codex: JSON-RPC lines from stdout → dir:out, stdin requests → dir:in
- Shell: capture deltas → dir:out (no stdin)

### DB migration 22
- Add `raw_log_file TEXT` column to sessions table
- Store JSONL path in session record

### Backfill command (`orka backfill <id>`)
- Read raw JSONL, filter dir:out lines
- Call adapter.replayRawLog() to re-derive ProviderRuntimeEvents
- Delete old orchestration_events for session
- Re-insert via engine.ingest()
- Add to OrkaService interface + RPC handler + CLI command

title: Add touch-friendly session search in mobile sidebar

title: Create useMobileBreakpoint hook
description:
## What
Create a shared React hook `useMobileBreakpoint()` that returns `{ isMobile: boolean }` based on a `768px` media query match. This hook will be consumed by multiple components to toggle between mobile and desktop layouts.

## Files
- `packages/dashboard/src/lib/useMobileBreakpoint.ts` — new file

## Details
- Use `window.matchMedia('(max-width: 767px)')` with an `addEventListener('change', ...)` pattern.
- Return `{ isMobile: boolean }` — true when viewport is below 768px.
- Clean up listener on unmount.
- SSR-safe: default to `false` if `window` is undefined (unlikely for this SPA, but good practice).
- 768px aligns with Tailwind's `md:` breakpoint (768px and up means desktop).

## Acceptance
- Hook correctly returns true on mobile-width viewports and false on desktop.
- Changing viewport width (e.g., DevTools responsive mode) triggers a re-render with the updated value.
- No memory leaks (listener cleanup on unmount).

title: Add Tailwind CSS utilities for mobile-specific spacing
Prevent body scroll when mobile sidebar drawer is open
description:
## What
When the mobile sidebar drawer is open, prevent the background content from scrolling. This is a common mobile UX pattern to avoid confusing dual-scroll behavior.

## Files
- \`packages/dashboard/src/components/MobileSidebarDrawer.tsx\`

## Details
- When the drawer opens, set \`document.body.style.overflow = 'hidden'\` and \`document.body.style.position = 'fixed'\` (or use \`overscroll-behavior: contain\` on the drawer).
- When the drawer closes, restore the original body styles.
- Clean up on component unmount to avoid leaving the body locked.
- A simpler approach: use \`overscroll-behavior: contain\` on the drawer's scroll container and \`touch-action: none\` on the backdrop. Test which approach works best on iOS Safari (which is notoriously tricky with scroll locking).
- Consider using a tiny utility hook: \`useScrollLock(isLocked: boolean)\`.

## Acceptance
- Background content does not scroll when the drawer is open on mobile.
- Scrolling inside the drawer's session list works normally.
- Body scroll is restored when the drawer closes.
- No scroll position jump when locking/unlocking (iOS Safari edge case).

title: Mobile-friendly ToolCallDetails expansion

title: Create mobile sidebar drawer overlay component
description:

title: Create mobile bottom tab bar navigation

title: Abstract tmux into a SessionRunner interface
description:
Currently tmux is deeply coupled as the session runner throughout orchestrator, CLI, and tmux.ts. Abstract it behind a SessionRunner interface so we can swap tmux for an internal process runner (like T3 Code's approach) without touching the rest of the codebase.

Interface sketch:
- spawn(name, script, cwd) → void
- kill(name) → void  
- has(name) → boolean
- list() → RunnerSession[]
- capture(name, lines?) → string
- sendKeys(name, keys) → void
- attach(name) → void

Implementations:
- TmuxRunner (current behavior)
- ProcessRunner (future: direct child_process/Bun.spawn, no tmux dependency)

Key files to refactor:
- packages/daemon/src/tmux.ts → interface + TmuxRunner
- packages/daemon/src/orchestrator.ts → use interface
- packages/cli/src/index.ts → attach via interface
- packages/daemon/src/local-client.ts → inject runner
close_reason: tmux abstracted behind SessionRunner interface, swappable via setRunner()

title: Map missing Claude Code system events — task_progress, hook_*, status, compact_boundary
description:
We're dropping several Claude Code system events that could be useful:

## Not mapped (from raw logs analysis)
- `system.task_progress` (3102 occurrences) — tool execution progress updates. Could show real-time progress in dashboard.
- `system.task_started` (131) — tool call started. Could show 'Reading file...' immediately.
- `system.task_notification` (131) — tool call completed with result summary.
- `system.hook_started` (132) — PreToolUse/PostToolUse hook firing.
- `system.hook_response` (132) — hook result (allow/deny).
- `system.status` (12) — Claude Code internal status changes.
- `system.compact_boundary` (6) — context window compaction happened.

## Priority
- task_progress/started/notification — HIGH (real-time tool execution visibility)
- hook events — MEDIUM (supervised mode debugging)
- status — LOW (internal)
- compact_boundary — LOW but interesting (shows when context was trimmed)

## Impact
These events are already captured in raw logs. We just need to map them in claude-adapter.ts mapClaudeEvent() and decide what OrchestrationEvent types they become.
